questions.stem:
In the context of schema normalization in relational DBMS, consider a set $F$ of functional dependencies. The set of all functional dependencies implied by $F$ is called the closure of $F$. To compute the closure of $F$, Armstrong's Axioms can be applied. Consider $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ as sets of attributes over a relational schema. The three rules of Armstrong's Axioms are described as follows.

Reflexivity: If $Y \subseteq X$, then $X \to Y$
Augmentation: If $X \to Y$, then $XZ \to YZ$ for any $Z$
Transitivity: If $X \to Y$ and $Y \to Z$, then $X \to Z$

The additional rule of Union is defined as follows.

Union: If $X \to Y$ and $X \to Z$, then $X \to YZ$

It can be proved that the additional rule of Union is also implied by the three rules of Armstrong's Axioms. Listed below are four combinations of these three rules. Which one of these combinations is both necessary and sufficient for the proof ?

steps.title: The three axioms in plain words
steps.body: A functional dependency $X \to Y$ says: any two rows that agree on every attribute of $X$ also agree on every attribute of $Y$. Armstrong's axioms are three moves for deriving new dependencies from known ones. Reflexivity: a set determines its own subsets. Augmentation: adding the same attributes to both sides keeps a dependency true. Transitivity: if $X$ fixes $Y$ and $Y$ fixes $Z$, then $X$ fixes $Z$. A proof uses a combination of these moves; a combination is necessary and sufficient when the proof needs every rule in it and needs nothing else.

steps.title: Derive Union from the given facts
steps.body: Given $X \to Y$ and $X \to Z$. Augment the first with $X$: $X \to XY$ (since $XX = X$). Augment the second with $Y$: $XY \to YZ$. Apply transitivity to $X \to XY$ and $XY \to YZ$ to get $X \to YZ$, which is Union.
steps.tex: X\to Y \Rightarrow X\to XY;\quad X\to Z \Rightarrow XY\to YZ;\quad X\to XY,\ XY\to YZ \Rightarrow X\to YZ

steps.title: Check that nothing else is needed or can be dropped
steps.body: The derivation used augmentation twice and transitivity once, and never needed Reflexivity. Dropping Augmentation leaves no way to build $XY$, and dropping Transitivity leaves no way to chain the two dependencies. So Augmentation and Transitivity are both necessary, and together they are sufficient. That is option (D).

shortcut.body: Union needs a bigger left side to chain: augment, augment, then transitivity. Reflexivity only creates trivial dependencies and plays no part, so the option that omits it is (D). Option (A) is sufficient but not necessary, because Reflexivity plays no part; option (B) is not even sufficient, because it has no Transitivity.

traps.text: Choosing the full set. It is sufficient, but Reflexivity is not necessary, and the question asks for necessary and sufficient.
Believing Union needs no chaining. Without Transitivity the two dependencies $X\to XY$ and $XY\to YZ$ can never be joined into $X\to YZ$.
Transitivity alone cannot build $XY$ on a left side; the step $X \to XY$ and $XY \to YZ$ both come from Augmentation.

recognize.clues: The stem asks which of the three Armstrong rules a proof of the derived Union rule needs, and the words "necessary and sufficient" mean you must also show that no listed rule can be dropped.
recognize.contrast: Attribute closure also derives dependencies, but it computes $X^+$ for one concrete set of attributes; here the rules are applied symbolically to arbitrary sets and the question is which rules are used.

check.body: Test necessity by removing rules. With only Reflexivity and Transitivity, the right sides reachable from $X \to Y$ and $X \to Z$ are subsets of $X$, of $Y$ or of $Z$, never $YZ$ for independent $Y$ and $Z$. Without Transitivity no rule combines two dependencies at all, so $X \to YZ$ cannot appear.

variation.stem: The Decomposition rule says: if $X \to YZ$ then $X \to Y$. It can be proved from the three rules of Armstrong's Axioms (Reflexivity, Augmentation, Transitivity). Which one of the following combinations is both necessary and sufficient for the proof?
variation.explanation: Since $Y \subseteq YZ$, Reflexivity gives $YZ \to Y$. Transitivity chains $X \to YZ$ with $YZ \to Y$ into $X \to Y$. Augmentation never appears, so Reflexivity and Transitivity are both needed and together enough.

questions.stem:
Let $P$, $Q$, $R$ and $S$ be the attributes of a relation in a relational schema. Let $X \longrightarrow Y$ indicate functional dependency in the context of a relational database, where $X, Y \subseteq \{P, Q, R, S\}$.

Which of the following options is/are always true?

steps.title: What a dependency claims
steps.body: $X \to Y$ holds when any two rows that agree on $X$ also agree on $Y$. A statement is always true only if it holds for every possible table, so one table that breaks it is enough to reject it. To accept a statement, derive it from Armstrong's axioms: augmentation (add the same attributes to both sides), transitivity, and the derived rules union and decomposition.

steps.title: Test each option
steps.body: (A): $PQ \to R$ and $P \to R$ say nothing about $Q$ alone. Rows $(P,Q,R) = (1,1,1)$ and $(2,1,2)$ satisfy both premises yet agree on $Q$ and differ on $R$, so $Q \to R$ fails. (B): with rows $(1,1,1)$, $(1,2,2)$, $(2,1,2)$ the pair $PQ$ is distinct in every row, so $PQ\to R$ holds, but $P=1$ gives $R=1,2$ and $Q=1$ gives $R=1,2$, so neither single dependency holds. (C): augment $P\to R$ by $Q$ to get $PQ\to RQ$, augment $Q \to S$ by $R$ to get $QR \to RS$, then chain: $PQ \to RS$. True. (D): augmenting $P\to R$ by $Q$ gives $PQ\to RQ$, and decomposition gives $PQ \to R$. True.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: Only (C) and (D) can be derived. The answer is C and D.

shortcut.body: A bigger left side never loses a dependency (D), and two dependencies side by side combine on the union of their left sides (C). A smaller left side is never guaranteed (A, B): hunt for a two-row counterexample.

traps.text: Reading $PQ\to R$ and $P\to R$ as if $Q$ were also enough. The second already explains $R$ without $Q$, so the first adds no information about $Q$.
Assuming a composite determinant splits into 'either part'. A pair can be a key while neither member is.

recognize.clues: The phrase "always true" about dependencies between attribute sets of a four-attribute relation, with no table given, means each option is a claim to derive from the axioms or to refute with a small table.
recognize.contrast: Checking FDs against an instance tests a dependency on one given table; here no table is given, so you either derive the statement or build the counterexample table yourself.

check.body: Small tables settle the false options: they break on tables of two or three rows. A brute-force enumeration of every table with up to three rows over four attributes and three values finds no table that breaks the other two statements, which agrees with their derivation by augmentation.

questions.stem: In the context of relational database normalization, which of the following statements is/are true?
options: It is always possible to obtain a dependency-preserving 3NF decomposition of a relation
It is always possible to obtain a dependency-preserving 1NF decomposition of a relation
It is not always possible to obtain a dependency-preserving BCNF decomposition of a relation
It is not always possible to obtain a dependency-preserving 2NF decomposition of a relation

steps.title: Terms
steps.body: A decomposition splits a relation into smaller ones. It is dependency preserving when every original dependency can be checked inside one piece (or follows from the dependencies kept in the pieces). Normal forms nest: BCNF implies 3NF implies 2NF implies 1NF. The tool to know is the 3NF synthesis algorithm: take a canonical cover, make one relation per dependency, add a candidate key if no relation holds one, and drop redundant relations. It always gives a lossless, dependency-preserving 3NF decomposition.

steps.title: Apply to each statement
steps.body: (A) is true by the synthesis algorithm. (B) is true: a relation in 1NF already, or any 3NF result, is also 1NF; the identity decomposition preserves every dependency. (C) is true: $R(A,B,C)$ with $AB\to C$ and $C\to B$ has no dependency-preserving BCNF decomposition, because $C\to B$ forces a split that loses $AB\to C$. (D) is false: every 3NF decomposition is also in 2NF, so a dependency-preserving 2NF decomposition always exists.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: Statements A, B and C are true; D is false because 2NF is weaker than 3NF.

shortcut.body: 3NF always works; BCNF sometimes cannot; anything weaker than 3NF therefore always works. So A, B, C true and D false.

traps.text: Thinking 2NF is harder than 3NF. It is weaker, and the 3NF synthesis result is already in 2NF.
Leaving out C because BCNF sounds like the 'best' form. The price of BCNF is that dependency preservation can be lost.

recognize.clues: Each statement asks whether a dependency-preserving decomposition always exists for 1NF, 2NF, 3NF or BCNF, which is what the synthesis guarantee and its BCNF counterpart decide.
recognize.contrast: BCNF decomposition always yields a lossless split but may lose dependencies, whereas synthesis keeps dependencies; the two guarantees differ and must not be swapped.

check.body: Recompute the BCNF counterexample. For $R(A,B,C)$ with $AB \to C$ and $C \to B$, the keys are $AB$ and $AC$. $C \to B$ has a non-key left side, so $R$ is not in BCNF. Splitting on it gives $(C,B)$ and $(A,C)$, and the only dependency visible inside the pieces is $C \to B$. The closure of $AB$ under $C \to B$ is just $AB$, so $AB \to C$ is lost.

variation.stem: Which of the following statements about normal forms of relations is/are TRUE?
options: Every relation in 3NF is also in BCNF
Every relation in BCNF is also in 3NF
Every relation with exactly two attributes is in BCNF
Every relation has a dependency-preserving BCNF decomposition
variation.explanation: BCNF asks for a superkey on the left of every non-trivial dependency, which is stricter than 3NF, so the second is true. With two attributes any non-trivial dependency has a single attribute on the left that determines the rest, so that attribute is a key, making the third true. $R(A,B,C)$ with $AB \to C$ and $C \to A$ is in 3NF (all attributes are prime) but not in BCNF, and it has no dependency-preserving BCNF decomposition, so the first and fourth are false.

questions.stem: Consider a relational database schema with a relation $R(A, B, C, D)$. If $\{A, B\}$ and $\{A, C\}$ are the only two candidate keys of the relation $R$, then the number of superkeys of relation $R$ is ______. (answer in integer)

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: A superkey is any set of attributes whose closure is all of $R$. A candidate key is a minimal superkey. Every superkey contains some candidate key, and every set containing a candidate key is a superkey. So the superkeys are exactly the sets that contain $\{A,B\}$ or contain $\{A,C\}$.

steps.title: Count with inclusion and exclusion
steps.body: Supersets of $\{A,B\}$ choose any subset of $\{C,D\}$: $2^2=4$. Supersets of $\{A,C\}$ choose any subset of $\{B,D\}$: $4$. Sets containing both keys contain $\{A,B,C\}$ and choose any subset of $\{D\}$: $2$. Add the two counts and subtract the overlap counted twice.

steps.title: List to confirm
steps.body: $AB$, $ABC$, $ABD$, $ABCD$ and $AC$, $ACD$: six sets. The answer is 6.

shortcut.body: Count supersets of each key ($2^{n-k}$ each), subtract supersets of their union: $4+4-2=6$.

traps.text: Answering 8 by adding the two counts and forgetting that $ABC$ and $ABCD$ contain both keys.
Answering 2 by counting only the candidate keys. Every superset of a key is also a superkey.

recognize.clues: Only the candidate keys are given and the question asks for the number of superkeys of a four-attribute relation, so it is a count of supersets of each key with the overlap handled once.
recognize.contrast: Finding candidate keys starts from a dependency set and needs closures; here the keys are already given and nothing needs closure, only counting.

check.body: Count by complement. Of the 16 subsets of $\{A,B,C,D\}$, a subset fails to be a superkey when it holds neither key. Those without $A$ number 8, and those with $A$ but neither $B$ nor $C$ number 2, so 10 fail and the remaining subsets are superkeys.

variation.stem: A relation $R(A, B, C, D, E)$ has exactly two candidate keys, $\{A, B\}$ and $\{C, D\}$. The number of superkeys of $R$ is ______. (answer in integer)

questions.stem:
Consider the following relational schema along with all the functional dependencies that hold on them.

$R1(A, B, C, D, E)$: $\{ D \to E,\ EA \to B,\ EB \to C \}$

$R2(A, B, C, D)$: $\{ A \to D,\ A \to B,\ C \to A \}$

Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: A candidate key is a smallest set of attributes whose closure is the whole relation. An attribute is prime if it belongs to some candidate key. A relation is in 3NF when every non-trivial dependency $X\to Y$ satisfies at least one of: $X$ is a superkey, or every attribute of $Y$ not in $X$ is prime. So find the keys first, then test each dependency.

steps.title: R1(A,B,C,D,E)
steps.body: $A$ and $D$ never appear on a right side, so both are in every key. $\{A,D\}^+$: $D\to E$ gives $E$, then $EA\to B$ gives $B$, then $EB\to C$ gives $C$. So $AD$ is the only candidate key and $A$, $D$ are the prime attributes. Test $D\to E$: $D$ is not a superkey and $E$ is not prime. This violates 3NF, so R1 is not in 3NF.

steps.title: R2(A,B,C,D)
steps.body: $C$ never appears on a right side, so it is in every key, and $C^+$: $C\to A$, then $A\to D$ and $A\to B$ give $\{C,A,D,B\}$. The only key is $C$ and the prime attribute is $C$. Test $A\to D$: $A$ is not a superkey ($A^+=ABD$) and $D$ is not prime. This violates 3NF, so R2 is not in 3NF.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: R1 and R2 are both not in 3NF: options C and D.

shortcut.body: Find the key (attributes on no right side), then look for one dependency whose left side is not a key and whose right side is non-prime. Both relations have one, so both fail 3NF.

traps.text: Seeing that $EA\to B$ and $EB\to C$ chain from the key and concluding 3NF. The failing dependency is the first one, $D\to E$, a partial dependency on part of the key.
Treating $C\to A$ as the only dependency that matters because $C$ is the key. $A\to D$ has a non-key left side and a non-prime right side.

recognize.clues: Two schemas come with full dependency lists and every option says "in 3NF" or "not in 3NF", so each relation needs its keys and a test of every dependency's left and right sides.
recognize.contrast: BCNF is stricter and ignores prime attributes, so a relation can pass 3NF through a prime right side yet fail BCNF; apply the prime-attribute escape before declaring a 3NF failure.

check.body: Look at the violations from another angle. In R1, $D \to E$ has $D$ as a proper part of the key $AD$, a partial dependency, which 2NF already forbids and 3NF therefore cannot allow. In R2, $C$ reaches $D$ only through $A$, a transitive path $C \to A \to D$ onto a non-prime attribute.

Consider the following relational schemas and the functional dependencies that hold on them.

$R1(A, B, C, D)$: $\{ A \to B,\ B \to C,\ C \to D \}$

$R2(A, B, C, D)$: $\{ AB \to C,\ C \to B,\ AB \to D \}$

Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?
variation.explanation: In R1 the only key is $A$, and $B \to C$ has a non-key left side and a non-prime right side, so R1 is not in 3NF. In R2 the keys are $AB$ and $AC$, so $A$, $B$, $C$ are prime. $AB \to C$ and $AB \to D$ have a key on the left and $C \to B$ has a prime right side, so R2 is in 3NF, but $C$ is not a superkey, so R2 is not in BCNF.

questions.stem:
Consider a relational schema $team(name, city, owner)$, with functional dependencies $\{name \to city,\ name \to owner\}$.

The relation $team$ is decomposed into two relations, $t1(name, city)$ and $t2(name, owner)$. Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?
options: The relation $team$ is NOT in BCNF.
The relations $t1$ and $t2$ are in BCNF.
The decomposition constitutes a lossless join.

steps.title: Terms and rules
steps.body: BCNF: for every non-trivial dependency $X\to Y$ in the relation, $X$ is a superkey. 3NF is the same unless $Y$ is prime. A decomposition into $R_1,R_2$ is lossless when the attributes the pieces share form a superkey of $R_1$ or of $R_2$; then joining the pieces gives back exactly the original rows.

steps.title: Is team in BCNF?
steps.body: $name^+=\{name,city,owner\}$, so $name$ is a key. Both dependencies have $name$ on the left, so every dependency has a key on the left. $team$ is in BCNF, and therefore also in 3NF. Statements (A) and (D) are false.

steps.title: Pieces and the join
steps.body: In $t1(name,city)$ the only dependency is $name\to city$ with $name$ a key; in $t2$ likewise. Both are in BCNF, so (B) is true. The shared attribute is $name$, which is a key of both pieces, so the join is lossless and (C) is true.

shortcut.body: One key, name, determines everything: the relation is already BCNF, and splitting on the key is lossless with BCNF pieces. B and C.

traps.text: Seeing two dependencies and assuming a violation. Both have the key on the left.
Same slip for 3NF: BCNF implies 3NF, so a relation in BCNF cannot fail 3NF.

recognize.clues: One relation is split into two pieces that share a single attribute, and the options ask about BCNF, 3NF and lossless join together, so test the original, each piece, and then the shared attribute.
recognize.contrast: Dependency preservation is a separate property that these options do not ask about; a lossless split can still lose dependencies, so do not infer one from the other.

check.body: Run the chase on two rows. The row for $t1$ is $(name, city, ?)$ and the row for $t2$ is $(name, ?, owner)$. They agree on $name$, so $name \to city$ and $name \to owner$ fill both unknowns and a row of known values appears, confirming the join is lossless.

variation.stem:
Consider a relational schema $emp(id, dept, mgr)$ with functional dependencies $\{id \to dept,\ dept \to mgr\}$.

The relation is decomposed into $e1(id, dept)$ and $e2(dept, mgr)$. Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE?
options: The relation $emp$ is NOT in BCNF.
The relations $e1$ and $e2$ are in BCNF.
The decomposition loses the implied dependency $id \to mgr$, so it is not dependency preserving.
variation.explanation: The only key is $id$, since $id^+ = \{id, dept, mgr\}$. In $emp$, $dept \to mgr$ has a non-key left side and a non-prime right side, so $emp$ is not in 3NF and hence not in BCNF. In each piece every dependency has a key on its left, so both are in BCNF. The dependency $id \to mgr$ follows from $id \to dept$ in $e1$ and $dept \to mgr$ in $e2$, so nothing is lost.

questions.stem:
A functional dependency $F: X \to Y$ is termed as a useful functional dependency if and only if it satisfies all the following three conditions:

- $X$ is not the empty set.
- $Y$ is not the empty set.
- Intersection of $X$ and $Y$ is the empty set.

For a relation $R$ with 4 attributes, the total number of possible useful functional dependencies is ________

steps.title: What is being counted
steps.body: A dependency is a pair $(X, Y)$ of attribute sets. Useful means both are non-empty and they share no attribute. So the count is the number of ordered pairs of disjoint, non-empty subsets of a 4-element set.

steps.title: Give each attribute one of three roles
steps.body: Each attribute goes to $X$, to $Y$, or to neither. That gives $3^4=81$ assignments with $X\cap Y=\varnothing$. Remove the assignments where $X$ is empty: each attribute is in $Y$ or neither, $2^4=16$. Remove those where $Y$ is empty: $16$. The all-neither assignment was removed twice, so add it back once.

steps.title: Cross-check by sizes
steps.body: Choose $|X|=i$ and $|Y|=j$ with $i,j\ge 1$, $i+j\le 4$. The count is the sum over $(i,j)$ of $\binom4i\binom{4-i}{j}$: $i=1$ gives $4(3+3+1)=28$, $i=2$ gives $6(2+1)=18$, $i=3$ gives $4\cdot 1=4$, total 50.

shortcut.body: Three choices per attribute, $3^n$, then subtract the two empty cases and add back the double-subtracted one: $3^n-2^{n+1}+1$. For $n=4$ it is 50.

traps.text: Answering 81: forgetting the non-empty conditions.
Answering 49: subtracting $2^4$ twice and forgetting to add the all-neither case back.
Answering 65: removing only the empty-$X$ assignments ($81-16$) and forgetting the empty-$Y$ ones.

recognize.clues: The question counts dependencies by structure alone (non-empty sides that are disjoint) with no dependency set given, so it is a counting problem over pairs of attribute subsets.
recognize.contrast: Counting superkeys also counts subsets of attributes, but those are single sets that determine everything; here each object is a pair of sets forming one dependency.

check.body: Try the formula where you can list everything. For 2 attributes it gives $3^2 - 2^3 + 1 = 2$, and only $A \to B$ and $B \to A$ qualify. For 3 attributes it gives 12, matching 6 dependencies with one attribute on each side plus 6 with one side of size two.

variation.stem: A functional dependency $X \to Y$ is useful if and only if $X$ is not empty, $Y$ is not empty, and $X$ and $Y$ have no attribute in common. For a relation with 5 attributes, the total number of useful functional dependencies is ______

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about a relation R in first normal form (1NF) is/are TRUE ?
options: R can have a multi-attribute key
R cannot have a foreign key
R cannot have a composite attribute
R cannot have more than one candidate key

steps.title: What 1NF demands
steps.body: A relation is in first normal form when every attribute value is atomic: one indivisible value per cell, with no set-valued, repeating or composite attribute. 1NF says nothing about keys: any number of candidate keys, composite keys, and foreign keys are allowed.

steps.title: Judge the options
steps.body: (A) A key of several attributes is fine: true. (B) Foreign keys are unrelated to atomicity: false. (C) A composite attribute such as an address with parts stored as one structured cell is not atomic, so R cannot have one: true. (D) A relation can have many candidate keys in 1NF: false. The answer is A and C.

shortcut.body: 1NF is only about atomic cells. Anything about keys is allowed; only composite or multi-valued attributes are banned.

traps.text: Linking foreign keys to a normal form. 1NF is silent on them.
Confusing 1NF with a single-key rule. Several candidate keys are legal at every normal form.

recognize.clues: The stem asks what a relation in 1NF can or cannot have, so every option is tested against the atomic-value rule alone.
recognize.contrast: Second normal form and above do restrict dependencies on keys, so their conditions must not be carried back to 1NF.

check.body: Test with a concrete table, Enroll(roll, course, email, grade), where every cell holds one value and each email belongs to one student. It has the composite candidate keys $(roll, course)$ and $(email, course)$, and $course$ can be a foreign key to another relation. It also has the partial dependency $roll \to email$. So 1NF allows composite keys, several candidate keys and foreign keys (A true, B and D false). Only replacing $email$ by a list of addresses breaks atomicity (C true).

questions.stem: The symbol $\to$ indicates functional dependency in the context of a relational database. Which of the following options is/are TRUE?
options: $((X, Y) \to Z$ and $W \to Y)$ implies $(X, W) \to Z$

steps.title: The rules
steps.body: $A\to B$ means rows that agree on $A$ agree on $B$. Valid derivations are: decomposition ($A\to BC$ gives $A\to B$), augmentation, and transitivity. A smaller left side cannot be assumed to work.

steps.title: Test each option
steps.body: (A) Removing $Y$ from the left side is not allowed. If $XY$ is a key and $X$ alone is not, $X \to ZW$ fails. False. (B) Decomposition of the right side: true. (C) $W\to Y$ gives $XW\to XY$ by augmentation, then $XY\to Z$ by transitivity gives $XW\to Z$. True. (D) Transitivity. True. The answer is B, C and D.

shortcut.body: Right side may shrink (B), left side may not. Chain through a shared set (C, D).

traps.text: Dropping an attribute from the left side. The pair may be the minimal key.

recognize.clues: Each option is an implication between dependencies written with attribute sets on both sides, and the stem asks which hold in general, so the test is whether a chain of Armstrong rules derives it.
recognize.contrast: Attribute closure answers the same question for one fixed set of dependencies. Here no concrete set is given, so closure has nothing to start from and you reason with the axioms or with a counterexample.

check.body: Check the failing option by counterexample. Take rows $(x, y_1, z_1, w_1)$ and $(x, y_2, z_2, w_2)$ with $y_1 \ne y_2$ and $z_1 \ne z_2$. They differ on $(X, Y)$, so $(X, Y) \to (Z, W)$ is not violated, yet they agree on $X$ and differ on $Z$, so $X \to (Z, W)$ fails. For each true option, no such pair can be built: any pair that agrees on the left side is forced to agree on the right side.

questions.stem: In a relational data model, which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: A relation with only two attributes is always in BCNF.
If all attributes of a relation are prime attributes, then the relation is in BCNF.
Every relation has at least one non-prime attribute.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: A prime attribute belongs to some candidate key. A relation is in BCNF when, for every non-trivial dependency $X\to Y$, the left side $X$ is a superkey. Having only prime attributes is the 3NF escape clause, not the BCNF rule.

steps.title: Option A
steps.body: With attributes $A,B$ the non-trivial dependencies are $A\to B$ and $B\to A$. If $A\to B$ holds, $A^+=AB$, so $A$ is a superkey; the same for $B\to A$. No dependency can have a non-superkey left side, so a two-attribute relation is always in BCNF.

steps.title: Why the others fail
steps.body: (B) $R(A,B,C)$ with $AB\to C$ and $C\to B$ has keys $AB$ and $AC$, so all attributes are prime and it is in 3NF, but $C\to B$ has the non-key $C$ on the left, so it is not BCNF. (C) A relation whose key is all its attributes has no non-prime attribute. (D) BCNF decomposition can lose dependencies, as in the example for B. The answer is (A).

shortcut.body: Two attributes cannot hide a violation: the left side of any non-trivial dependency is the other attribute's determinant, hence a key. Pick A.

traps.text: Mixing up 3NF and BCNF. All-prime attributes is enough for 3NF, not for BCNF.
Assuming a relation always has a non-key attribute. An all-key relation has none.
Remembering that BCNF always lossless but forgetting dependency preservation is not guaranteed.

recognize.clues: The stem is a general true-or-false about normal forms, with statements built on words like "always", "only two attributes" and "all prime", so each one is checked against the BCNF definition or a counterexample.
recognize.contrast: 3NF and BCNF differ only in the prime-attribute escape. A statement that leans on prime attributes is really a 3NF statement and says nothing certain about BCNF.

check.body: Enumerate the two-attribute case. With attributes $A, B$ the only non-trivial dependencies are $A \to B$ and $B \to A$, so there are four possible dependency sets: none, either one, or both. In each, a left side that determines the other attribute has closure $AB$ and is a superkey, and with no dependencies there is nothing to violate. So no two-attribute relation can fail BCNF.

questions.stem:
Consider a relation $R(A, B, C, D, E)$ with the following three functional dependencies.

$AB \to C;\ BC \to D;\ C \to E;$

The number of superkeys in the relation $R$ is _____________.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: A superkey is a set whose closure is all attributes. Any set that contains a superkey is a superkey. The count equals the number of supersets of the candidate keys, so find the keys first.

steps.title: Find the key
steps.body: $A$ and $B$ appear on no right side, so every key contains both. $\{A,B\}^+$: $AB\to C$ gives $C$; $BC\to D$ gives $D$; $C\to E$ gives $E$. So $AB$ is the only candidate key.

steps.title: Count supersets
steps.body: Every superkey is $AB$ plus any subset of $\{C,D,E\}$: $2^3=8$.

shortcut.body: One key of $k$ attributes in $n$ gives $2^{n-k}$ superkeys: $2^{5-2}=8$.

traps.text: Answering 1: counting only the candidate key and forgetting its supersets.
Answering 32: counting all subsets of the five attributes.

recognize.clues: The stem asks for the number of superkeys rather than the keys themselves, with dependencies over five attributes, so the plan is to find the candidate keys and count the sets that contain one.
recognize.contrast: A candidate-key question wants only the minimal sets. Superkey counting wants every superset, and when there are several keys their supersets overlap and each set must be counted once.

check.body: Count by size instead of by formula. The key has two attributes, so there is 1 superkey of size two. Adding one of the other three attributes gives 3 of size three, adding two gives 3 of size four, and adding all three gives 1 of size five. Summing these four counts must reproduce the earlier total, and no set that misses $A$ or $B$ can be included because each of those has a closure short of the full relation.

Adding attributes to a superkey keeps it a superkey, so the superkeys are exactly the sets that contain a candidate key. Find the candidate keys first, then count the sets built on them.

Look for attributes that never appear on the right side of a dependency: they must sit inside every key. Close that set. If it reaches everything, it is the only key, and the remaining attributes can be added in any combination.

Consider a relation $R(A, B, C, D, E, F)$ with the following functional dependencies.

$AB \to C;\ C \to B;\ D \to E;$

variation.explanation: $A$, $D$ and $F$ appear on no right side, so every key contains them. Adding $B$ gives $ABDF$, which reaches $C$ and $E$; adding $C$ instead gives $ACDF$, which reaches $B$ and $E$. questions.stem:
Suppose the following functional dependencies hold on a relation $U$ with attributes $P, Q, R, S$, and $T$:

$P \to QR$
$RS \to T$

Which of the following functional dependencies can be inferred from the above functional dependencies?

steps.title: The tool: attribute closure
steps.body: The closure $X^+$ is the set of all attributes that $X$ determines. Start with $X$; whenever the left side of a given dependency lies inside the set, add its right side; repeat until nothing grows. A dependency $X\to Y$ is implied exactly when $Y\subseteq X^+$.

steps.title: Close each left side
steps.body: $P^+$: $P\to QR$ gives $\{P,Q,R\}$; $RS$ is not inside, so stop. $PS^+$: $\{P,S\}$ then $QR$ added gives $\{P,S,Q,R\}$, then $RS\to T$ applies and gives $\{P,Q,R,S,T\}$. $R^+=\{R\}$ because no left side lies inside $\{R\}$.

steps.title: Read off
steps.body: (A) $T\in PS^+$: yes. (B) $T\in R^+$: no. (C) $R\in P^+$: yes. (D) $Q\in PS^+$: yes. The answer is A, C and D.

shortcut.body: Close $PS$: P brings Q and R, then R with S brings T. That covers A and D; C is part of $P^+$. B needs S as well and is false.

traps.text: Using $RS\to T$ with only $R$. Both $R$ and $S$ must be present.

recognize.clues: The stem gives a short list of dependencies and asks which other dependencies can be inferred, so each option is an implication to test by closing its left side.
recognize.contrast: Armstrong's axioms also prove implications, but with named attributes and a fixed set of dependencies a closure is shorter and cannot skip a step.

check.body: Back-check the rejected option with a counterexample. Take two rows $(p_1, q_1, r, s_1, t_1)$ and $(p_2, q_2, r, s_2, t_2)$ with $s_1 \ne s_2$ and $t_1 \ne t_2$. They differ on $P$, so $P \to QR$ holds, and they differ on $S$, so $RS \to T$ holds. Yet they agree on $R$ and differ on $T$, so $R \to T$ is not forced.

questions.stem:
Consider the relation $R(P, Q, S, T, X, Y, Z, W)$ with the following functional dependencies.

$PQ \to X;\ P \to YX;\ Q \to Y;\ Y \to ZW$

Consider the decomposition of the relation $R$ into the constituent relations according to the following two decomposition schemes.

$D_1$: $R = [(P, Q, S, T);\ (P, T, X);\ (Q, Y);\ (Y, Z, W)]$
$D_2$: $R = [(P, Q, S);\ (T, X);\ (Q, Y);\ (Y, Z, W)]$

Which one of the following options is correct?
options: $D_1$ is a lossless decomposition, but $D_2$ is a lossy decomposition.
$D_1$ is a lossy decomposition, but $D_2$ is a lossless decomposition.

solutionDiagram.alt: Two chase tables, one for D1 and one for D2, each at the start and after applying the dependencies. In D1 the first row becomes all a, in D2 no row does.

steps.title: Lossless join in plain words
steps.body: A decomposition is lossless when joining the pieces back gives exactly the original relation, with no extra rows. The test with several pieces is the chase. Build a table with one row per piece and one column per attribute. Write the symbol $a$ where the piece contains the attribute and a distinct symbol $b_i$ otherwise. Then apply each functional dependency: if two rows agree on the left side, make them agree on the right side, preferring $a$. The decomposition is lossless if some row becomes all $a$.

steps.title: Chase D1
steps.body: Rows: $R_1(PQST)$, $R_2(PTX)$, $R_3(QY)$, $R_4(YZW)$. $Q\to Y$: $R_1$ and $R_3$ share $Q=a$, so $R_1$ gets $Y=a$. $Y\to ZW$: $R_1,R_3,R_4$ share $Y=a$, so $R_1$ gets $Z=W=a$. $P\to YX$: $R_1,R_2$ share $P=a$, so $R_1$ already has $Y=a$, and $R_1$ gets $X=a$ from $R_2$. Now $R_1$ is $(a,a,a,a,a,a,a,a)$. $D_1$ is lossless.

steps.title: Chase D2
steps.body: Rows: $R_1(PQS)$, $R_2(TX)$, $R_3(QY)$, $R_4(YZW)$. $Q\to Y$ and $Y\to ZW$ turn $R_1$ into $P,Q,S,Y,Z,W$ all $a$, but $T$ and $X$ stay $b$. The other dependencies $PQ\to X$ and $P\to YX$ need two rows that agree on $P$, and only $R_1$ has $P=a$. $R_2$ never gets $P,Q,S$. No row becomes all $a$, so $D_2$ is lossy. The drawing shows both tables.

steps.title: Check by keys
steps.body: The key of $R$ is $PQST$ (the closure of $PQST$ is everything and no attribute of it is derivable). $D_1$ keeps the whole key in one piece $R_1$ and each later piece hangs off by dependencies; $D_2$ splits $T$ away from $PQS$ with no common attribute, so rows of $T$ can pair with any $PQS$ row. The answer is (A).

shortcut.body: Find the key: $PQST$. A decomposition that has a piece containing the whole key and closes up through the dependencies is lossless; one that separates $T$ from $PQS$ with no shared attribute is lossy. $D_1$ lossless, $D_2$ lossy: A.

traps.text: Reversing the chase: $D_2$ looks tidy because every attribute is covered, but $T,X$ share no attribute with the other pieces.
Trusting that covering every attribute is enough. Lossless needs the join attributes to determine something.
Concluding D1 is lossy because $S$ appears in only one piece. It sits in $R_1$, the piece that holds the key, which is harmless.

recognize.clues: Both schemes split one relation into four pieces and the question compares whether the join is exact, with dependencies over all eight attributes, so the chase table is the right tool.
recognize.contrast: For a split into exactly two pieces, a shared set that is a key of one piece is enough. With more than two pieces that shortcut does not apply directly, and the chase is the safe test.

check.body: Pairwise merge test. For $D_1$ join the pieces one at a time, each time checking that the shared attributes determine all of one side. $(P,Q,S,T)$ and $(P,T,X)$ share $PT$, and $P \to X$ so $PT$ determines $(P,T,X)$. Joining $(Q,Y)$ shares $Q$, and $Q \to Y$. Joining $(Y,Z,W)$ shares $Y$, and $Y \to ZW$. Every step is lossless. For $D_2$, take two rows of $R$ with the same $S$ but different $P, Q, T, X$: the pieces $(P,Q,S)$ and $(T,X)$ share no attribute, so their join is a cross product and pairs $P,Q$ of one row with $T,X$ of the other, a row that $P \to X$ shows was never in $R$.

questions.stem: Consider a relational table $R$ that is in 3NF, but not in BCNF. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: $R$ has a nontrivial functional dependency $X \to A$, where $X$ is not a superkey and $A$ is a prime attribute.
$R$ has a nontrivial functional dependency $X \to A$, where $X$ is not a superkey and $A$ is a non-prime attribute and $X$ is not a proper subset of any key.
$R$ has a nontrivial functional dependency $X \to A$, where $X$ is not a superkey and $A$ is a non-prime attribute and $X$ is a proper subset of some key.
A cell in $R$ holds a set instead of an atomic value.

steps.title: The two definitions
steps.body: BCNF: for every non-trivial $X\to A$, $X$ is a superkey. 3NF: for every non-trivial $X\to A$, either $X$ is a superkey, or $A$ is prime (belongs to a candidate key). So 3NF is BCNF with one extra escape.

steps.title: What 'in 3NF but not BCNF' forces
steps.body: Not BCNF means some non-trivial $X\to A$ has $X$ not a superkey. Being in 3NF means that same dependency escapes through the second clause, so $A$ must be prime. So the relation has a non-trivial dependency with a non-superkey left side and a prime right side. That is option (A).

steps.title: Eliminate the rest
steps.body: (B) and (C) describe a non-prime $A$ with a non-superkey $X$, which is a direct 3NF violation (C is also a 2NF violation). (D) describes a violation of 1NF. The answer is (A).

shortcut.body: 3NF but not BCNF means the only escape used was 'right side is prime'. Pick the option that says prime.

traps.text: Option B is what a 3NF violation looks like; it cannot occur in a 3NF relation.
Option C is a partial dependency, which breaks 2NF and so 3NF.
Option D is about atomicity, which belongs to 1NF, and says nothing about the BCNF gap.

recognize.clues: The premise "in 3NF but not in BCNF" sets the two definitions side by side, and the options differ in whether the right side is prime and where the left side sits relative to a key.
recognize.contrast: A partial dependency (left side inside a key, right side non-prime) breaks 2NF and so 3NF. It is not the gap between 3NF and BCNF.

check.body: Test with a concrete relation. $R(A, B, C)$ with $AB \to C$ and $C \to B$ has candidate keys $AB$ and $AC$, so $B$ is prime. The dependency $C \to B$ fails BCNF but passes 3NF. It has a non-superkey left side and a prime right side, and the relation has no dependency with a non-prime right side and a non-superkey left side, which is what a 3NF violation would need.

questions.stem:
Let the set of functional dependencies $F = \{QR \to S,\ R \to P,\ S \to Q\}$ hold on a relation schema $X = (PQRS)$. $X$ is not in BCNF. Suppose $X$ is decomposed into two schemas $Y$ and $Z$, where $Y = (PR)$ and $Z = (QRS)$.

Consider the two statements given below.

I. Both $Y$ and $Z$ are in BCNF
II. Decomposition of $X$ into $Y$ and $Z$ is dependency preserving and lossless

Which of the above statements is/are correct?

solutionDiagram.alt: Relation X(PQRS) split into Y(PR) holding R to P and Z(QRS) holding QR to S and S to Q, with R as the shared attribute and a note that Z is not in BCNF but the split is lossless and dependency preserving.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body: BCNF: every non-trivial dependency in a relation has a superkey on the left. A dependency of $F$ belongs to a piece when all its attributes lie in that piece, and the projected dependencies of a piece are all dependencies of $F^+$ inside it. A decomposition is lossless when the shared attributes form a key of one piece, and dependency preserving when every original dependency can be derived from the dependencies kept within the pieces.

steps.title: Statement I: are Y and Z in BCNF?
steps.body: In $Y=(P,R)$ the dependency is $R\to P$ and $R^+=PR$, a key of $Y$, so $Y$ is in BCNF. In $Z=(Q,R,S)$ the dependencies are $QR\to S$ and $S\to Q$. Now $S^+$ inside $Z$ is $\{S,Q\}$, which does not contain $R$, so $S$ is not a key of $Z$ and $S\to Q$ violates BCNF. Statement I is false.

steps.title: Statement II: lossless and preserving
steps.body: The shared attribute is $R$. $R^+=\{R,P\}$ contains all of $Y$, so $R$ is a key of $Y$ and the join is lossless. $R\to P$ is inside $Y$, and $QR\to S$ and $S\to Q$ are inside $Z$. All three dependencies are kept, so the decomposition is dependency preserving. Statement II is true.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: Only II is correct: option (C). The drawing shows where each dependency lives.

shortcut.body: Check II first, since it is fast: shared attribute $R$ is a key of $Y$, and every FD fits in $Y$ or $Z$. Then find one BCNF violator in $Z$ ($S\to Q$) to kill I. Answer C.

traps.text: Assuming a lossless, dependency-preserving split is also BCNF. $Z$ still contains $S\to Q$ with a non-key left side.
Calling $S \to Q$ fine because $S$ determines something. $S$ is not a key of $Z$.
Rejecting II because the decomposition looks lossy. $R$ is a key of $Y$, so the join is lossless.

recognize.clues: The question gives a schema, its dependencies and a specific two-way split, then asks about BCNF of the pieces together with lossless join and dependency preservation, the three tests of a decomposition.
recognize.contrast: Lossless join and dependency preservation are independent of BCNF: a split can have both properties and still leave a piece that violates BCNF.

check.body: Check the lossless claim on instance rows. Because $R \to P$, each value of $R$ in $Y$ carries one value of $P$, so every row of $Z$ matches exactly one row of $Y$ in the join and nothing extra appears. For the BCNF claim on $Z$, the rows $(q, r_1, s)$ and $(q, r_2, s)$ can both occur, since $QR \to S$ is not violated by them. They agree on $S$ and differ on $R$, so $S$ is not a key of $Z$.

hints.text: There are two separate claims, so run two separate checks: whether each piece is in BCNF, and whether the split loses information or dependencies. Settle each statement on its own.

A piece is in BCNF when every non-trivial dependency that holds inside it has a superkey of that piece on the left. A dependency holds inside a piece when it follows from $F$ and uses only that piece's attributes.

A two-way split is lossless when the shared attributes determine all of one piece. It preserves dependencies when every original dependency can be recovered from the dependencies that live inside single pieces.

List the attributes of each piece, then write which of the three given dependencies fit entirely inside it. Compute closures of the left sides inside that piece to judge whether they are superkeys of that piece.
Find the attributes shared by $Y$ and $Z$ and compute their closure under $F$. See whether that closure covers all of $Y$ or all of $Z$.

Let the set of functional dependencies $F = \{AB \to C,\ C \to A,\ C \to D\}$ hold on a relation schema $X = (ABCD)$. $X$ is not in BCNF. Suppose $X$ is decomposed into two schemas $Y$ and $Z$, where $Y = (ACD)$ and $Z = (BC)$.

Consider the two statements given below.

I. Both $Y$ and $Z$ are in BCNF
II. Decomposition of $X$ into $Y$ and $Z$ is dependency preserving and lossless

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
variation.explanation: In $Y$ the attribute $C$ determines $A$ and $D$, so it is a key and $Y$ is in BCNF; $Z$ has only trivial dependencies, so statement I is true. The join is lossless because the shared $C$ is a key of $Y$. But $AB \to C$ needs $A$ and $B$ in one piece, and $C \to A$, $C \to D$ cannot rebuild it, so the split is not dependency preserving and statement II is false.

questions.stem:
Consider the following four relational schemas. For each schema, all non-trivial functional dependencies are listed. The underlined attributes are the respective primary keys.

Schema I: Registration(rollno, courses)
Field 'courses' is a set-valued attribute containing the set of courses a student has registered for.
Non-trivial functional dependency: rollno $\to$ courses

Schema II: Registration(rollno, courseid, email)
Non-trivial functional dependencies:
rollno, courseid $\to$ email
email $\to$ rollno

Schema III: Registration(rollno, courseid, marks, grade)
Non-trivial functional dependencies:
rollno, courseid $\to$ marks, grade
marks $\to$ grade

Schema IV: Registration(rollno, courseid, credit)
Non-trivial functional dependencies:
rollno, courseid $\to$ credit
courseid $\to$ credit

Which one of the relational schemas above is in 3NF but not in BCNF?

solutionDiagram.alt: Table with one row per schema giving its keys, the offending dependency, the reason and the verdict; Schema II is highlighted as 3NF but not BCNF.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: 1NF: all cells atomic. 2NF: no non-prime attribute depends on part of a key. 3NF: every non-trivial $X\to A$ has $X$ a superkey or $A$ prime. BCNF: every non-trivial $X\to A$ has $X$ a superkey. A prime attribute is part of some candidate key. We want a schema where some dependency fails BCNF but escapes through prime attributes.

steps.title: Schema by schema
steps.body: I: 'courses' is set-valued, so it is not even in 1NF. II: candidate keys are $\{rollno,courseid\}$ and $\{email,courseid\}$ (since $email\to rollno$). The dependency $email\to rollno$ has a non-superkey left side but $rollno$ is prime, so 3NF holds and BCNF fails. III: $marks\to grade$ with $marks$ not a key and $grade$ non-prime: not 3NF. IV: $courseid\to credit$ is a partial dependency of a non-prime attribute on part of the key: not even 2NF.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: Only Schema II is in 3NF but not in BCNF: option (B). The table in the drawing lists the verdicts.

shortcut.body: Look for the dependency that points back into a key attribute. Only $email\to rollno$ does: B.

traps.text: Overlooking the set-valued attribute. Without atomic cells the schema is not in 1NF.
Treating $marks\to grade$ as a harmless transitive dependency. A non-key determines a non-prime attribute, which breaks 3NF.
Treating $courseid\to credit$ as BCNF-only. It is a partial dependency, so 2NF already fails.

recognize.clues: The stem asks for the schema whose highest normal form is 3NF, given each schema's complete dependency list and primary key, so every schema must be classified by the 1NF, 2NF, 3NF and BCNF tests in turn.
recognize.contrast: The gap between 3NF and BCNF is made only by dependencies with a prime right side. A violation with a non-prime right side already fails 3NF, and one with a partial key on the left already fails 2NF.

check.body: Redundancy table for Schema II. Insert $(1, c_1, e)$ and $(1, c_2, e)$. The fact $e \to 1$ (the email $e$ belongs to roll number 1) is now stored in both rows, which BCNF forbids since $e$ is not a superkey. The other schemas fail earlier: Schema I breaks 1NF with a set in one cell, Schema III breaks 3NF through $marks \to grade$ with a non-prime right side, and Schema IV breaks 2NF through the partial dependency $courseid \to credit$.

hints.text: Classify each of the four schemas by the highest normal form it reaches, then pick the one that passes 3NF and fails BCNF. Start by finding the candidate keys of each.

BCNF needs every non-trivial dependency to have a superkey on the left. 3NF also lets a dependency through when its right side is a prime attribute. 2NF forbids a non-prime attribute depending on part of a key, and 1NF needs atomic cells.

A schema is in 3NF but not BCNF only when some dependency has a non-superkey on the left and a prime attribute on the right. For each dependency that fails the superkey test, ask whether its right side is prime or non-prime.

For each schema, list the candidate keys by closure (a dependency can create a second key), mark the prime attributes, and test every listed dependency: is the left side a superkey, and if not, is the right side prime? Also check that the cells are atomic.

questions.stem:
The following functional dependencies hold true for the relational schema $R\{V, W, X, Y, Z\}$:

$V \to W$
$VW \to X$
$Y \to VX$
$Y \to Z$

Which of the following is irreducible equivalent for this set of functional dependencies?

steps.title: What irreducible means
steps.body: An irreducible (canonical) cover is an equivalent set of dependencies with single attributes on the right, no extraneous attribute on any left side, and no redundant dependency. Two sets are equivalent when each dependency of one follows from the other, checked with attribute closure.

steps.title: Reduce the given set
steps.body: Split right sides: $V\to W$, $VW\to X$, $Y\to V$, $Y\to X$, $Y\to Z$. In $VW\to X$, $W$ is extraneous because $V^+$ already contains $W$ and so $V\to X$ holds: replace it with $V\to X$. Now $Y\to X$ follows from $Y\to V$ and $V\to X$, so it is redundant. The result is $V\to W$, $V\to X$, $Y\to V$, $Y\to Z$.
steps.tex: \{V\to W,\ V\to X,\ Y\to V,\ Y\to Z\}

steps.title: Match the options
steps.body: That set is option (A). Option (B) uses $W\to X$, which is not implied ($W^+=W$). Option (C) keeps the redundant $Y\to X$. Option (D) has both faults.

shortcut.body: Look for $VW\to X$ and drop $W$ (since $V\to W$), then drop $Y\to X$ (since $Y\to V\to X$). Four dependencies remain: A.

traps.text: Replacing $VW\to X$ by $W\to X$ instead of $V\to X$. $W$ alone does not determine $X$.
Stopping before removing the redundant $Y\to X$, which follows by transitivity.
Making both mistakes of B and C.

recognize.clues: The words "irreducible equivalent" ask for a canonical cover. Two clues show the work: $VW\to X$ has two attributes on the left, and $Y\to VX$ combines targets that other dependencies may already reach.
recognize.contrast: Checking equivalence alone (each dependency of one set follows from the other) is not enough here, because option C is equivalent too; irreducibility also demands single right sides, no extraneous left attribute and no redundant dependency.

check.body: Check equivalence by closures. In the chosen set, $V^+=\{V,W,X\}$ and $Y^+=\{Y,V,W,X,Z\}$, so $VW\to X$, $Y\to VX$ and $Y\to Z$ all follow. Check minimality by deleting each dependency in turn: dropping $V\to X$ leaves $V^+=\{V,W\}$, dropping $Y\to V$ leaves $Y^+=\{Y,Z\}$, dropping $V\to W$ or $Y\to Z$ loses $W$ or $Z$. Every deletion loses information, so none is redundant.

hints.text: What three things must be true of a set of dependencies before it counts as irreducible, and which of the four given dependencies might break each one?
Recall what an extraneous attribute is: one on the left side that can be deleted without changing what the set implies. Attribute closure is the tool that tests it.
A dependency is redundant when the rest of the set already implies it, so removing it leaves the closure of every left side unchanged. Test it by computing a closure without that dependency.
Split every right side to a single attribute first. Then look at the dependency with two attributes on the left and ask whether the closure of one of them already contains the other.
Compute $V^+$ under the given set. It contains $W$, so one left-hand attribute of the two-attribute dependency can be dropped. Then check which dependency from $Y$ is now implied by a chain.

$B \to C$
$CA \to D$
$E \to AC$

options:
